title: Car Insurance After a Driving Ban: Getting Your Licence Back, What to Declare and How Premiums Recover
description: Car insurance after a UK driving ban: the D27 or D1 licence return, the High Risk Offender medical, what to declare, year-1 costs, and how premiums fall.
author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: You can't drive until the ban officially ends **and** you hold a valid licence again. Applying early doesn't give you any right to drive sooner.
The DVLA sends a **D27** renewal form about **56 days** before a ban ends, or **90 days** before for High Risk Offenders, who also need a medical. A **D1** form from the Post Office is the fallback.
Expect a large first-year loading. A drink-driving ban typically means around **£1,300+** in the first year with specialists, falling each year.
A disqualification is **spent when the ban ends**, but the endorsement's **5-year** period usually applies too. Declare the conviction until then.
Mainstream comparison sites often return no quotes, so go to specialist brokers and [non-standard auto insurance](/glossary/non-standard-auto-insurance) providers.

faqs.question: Can I get car insurance straight after a driving ban?
faqs.answer: Yes, from specialist insurers, once your licence is valid again. Expect high first-year premiums. See the [car insurance for high-risk and convicted drivers](/learn/car-insurance-for-high-risk-and-convicted-drivers) hub.

faqs.question: How long do I have to declare a driving ban?
faqs.answer: Until the conviction is spent, usually 5 years from conviction for adults because of the endorsement, or longer if the ban itself was longer than 5 years.

faqs.question: Do I need a medical to get my licence back?
faqs.answer: Only if you're a High Risk Offender, for example 2.5 times the limit or more, two drink-drive bans within 10 years, or failing or refusing to provide a specimen.

content.text: Coming back from a ban means two things: getting a valid licence and finding an insurer that will accept a disqualified driver. This guide is part of our [car insurance for high-risk and convicted drivers](/learn/car-insurance-for-high-risk-and-convicted-drivers) series. It covers bans for drink driving, [totting up](/glossary/totting-up) and serious offences in England, Wales and Scotland.

items: **Wait for the D27.** The DVLA usually posts it about 56 days before the ban ends (90 days for High Risk Offenders). If it doesn't arrive, use a **D1** from a Post Office.
**High Risk Offenders** (2.5 times the limit or more, two drink-drive bans within 10 years, or failing or refusing to provide a specimen) must pass a **DVLA medical** before the licence is returned.
**Extended retest:** if the court ordered one, for example after dangerous driving, you must pass it before driving unsupervised.
**New drivers:** a revocation under the New Drivers Act means retaking both tests. See [6 points in your first 2 years](/qa/what-happens-if-you-get-6-points-in-your-first-2-years).

content.text: Step 2: Finding Insurance as a Previously Banned Driver

Insurers ask about disqualifications and motoring convictions, usually over the last 5 years. Many mainstream insurers decline banned drivers. See [can an insurance company refuse to insure you](/qa/can-an-insurance-company-refuse-to-insure-you). Specialist brokers will quote. A drink-drive ban typically starts at roughly double a clean-licence premium. See [how long do motoring convictions stay on your licence](/qa/how-long-do-motoring-convictions-stay-on-your-licence) for how the loading fades, and [car insurance with points on your licence](/qa/can-you-get-car-insurance-with-points-on-your-licence) for points-only bans.

content.title: Driving While Disqualified Voids Any Insurance
content.text: No policy covers a disqualified driver. Driving during a ban adds a new conviction, can lead to imprisonment, and usually brings an IN10 for no insurance as well. See [is it against the law to drive without insurance](/qa/is-it-against-the-law-to-drive-without-insurance).
Step 3: What to Declare and When to Stop

Under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act, a disqualification is spent when the ban ends, but the 5-year endorsement period usually applies too, so the longer period wins. For a 12-month drink-driving ban, that means declaring the conviction for 5 years from conviction, even though the DR10 stays on your licence for 11. Full rules: [do you have to declare spent convictions](/qa/do-you-have-to-declare-spent-convictions-for-car-insurance). Non-motoring convictions are a separate question. See [which insurance companies do not ask about criminal convictions](/qa/which-insurance-companies-do-not-ask-about-criminal-convictions). If you'll be a named driver on someone else's policy, read [named driver with a conviction](/qa/can-a-driver-with-a-conviction-be-a-named-driver).
Step 4: Keep the First Policy Affordable

items: Pick a cheap-to-insure car. Think carefully before also taking on a write-off. See [are Cat N cars more expensive to insure](/qa/are-cat-n-cars-more-expensive-to-insure).
Choose a sensible voluntary [excess](/learn/what-is-an-excess), modelled with the [Car Insurance Deductible Calculator](/car-insurance-deductible-calculator/).
Consider telematics to prove safe driving.
Completing a drink-drive rehabilitation course shortens the ban, and some specialists credit it at renewal.
Re-quote every year, and in the month the conviction becomes spent.
